description:
Solo team. I'm a Geography (B.Sc.) student in Munich with a focus on GIS and Earth observation data. I work with Python, R and QGIS and have experience in geo data analysis and open mapping (Humanitarian OpenStreetMap Team / Missing Maps).

I'm working alone and am not looking for additional team members, but I'm happy to exchange ideas with other participants.
summary: Most tools show what changed. I show how long you need to wait before you can trust it. Trend Detective is an interactive web page for Europe, built on NASA POWER data (MERRA-2, SRB, CERES). For 315 grid cells and 44 years (1981–2024) it shows what is changing, where, how much, and whether the change is significant (Theil–Sen, Mann–Kendall, FDR correction). The new part is the time dimension: how many years of data a trend needs before it can be trusted. Half of the places with significant warming needed 21 years or fewer, while rainfall trends are almost nowhere detectable yet. In Oslo, a 10-year window even shows cooling (−0.27 °C per decade), while 44 years show +0.31 °C per decade. This matters for water managers, city planners and teachers: a rainfall cell without a clear trend does not mean “no change”. Validation against station data is shown openly, including where it fails. Nothing on the page is a forecast.
details:
What it does and how it works: Trend Detective is an interactive web page for Europe. It is built on NASA POWER monthly data (MERRA-2 meteorology, SRB and CERES sunshine) from 1981 to 2024 for 315 grid cells. For every cell it shows what is changing (air temperature, precipitation, root-zone soil moisture, water vapour in the air, relative humidity and sunshine at the ground, plus unusual warm, cold, wet and dry months and experimental daily extremes), where, how much, and whether the change is significant. Trends are estimated with the Theil–Sen slope and tested with the Mann–Kendall test, with FDR correction across cells. The new part is the time dimension of certainty: “years needed” is the shortest record, counted back from 2024, whose trend is significant and stays significant. A second map shows the year in which each trend first became detectable. Users click a place, search a town or enter their birth year to see what has changed since then.

Benefits and intended impact: Half of the places with significant warming needed 21 years of data or fewer, while rainfall trends are almost nowhere detectable yet. In Oslo, a 10-year window shows cooling (−0.27 °C per decade) while 44 years show +0.31 °C. The page makes this visible so that water managers, city planners and teachers can see where a trend can already be trusted and where more years of data are needed. A rainfall cell without a clear trend does not mean “no change”. A planner view shows how long one would have to measure to detect a trend of a given size.

Tools: Python (NumPy, pandas, SciPy) turns NASA POWER data into static JavaScript data files. The page itself is plain HTML, JavaScript and SVG, with no server, no login and no tracking. It runs on GitHub Pages, and a single-file offline copy is included. Code: MIT licence, all sources with attribution. I developed it together with Claude (Anthropic). Code and documentation: https://github.com/schumacherjan-dev/trend-detective

Creativity: Instead of one more trend map, the page maps how long we must wait for certainty. It includes a “Surprise me” button, warming stripes per place, a timelapse of when trends emerged, and links to every view.

Factors considered: I validated against measured series (DWD, SMHI, Met Office, Met Éireann, Berkeley Earth) and show where it fails: German precipitation matches in its yearly swings (r = 0.85) but not in the direction of the trend. Robustness checks (autocorrelation, placebo test, start-year test) are reported. Daily extremes are marked experimental and not validated against stations. Nothing on the page is a forecast. The page offers dark mode, keyboard use of the map and colour palettes checked for colour-vision deficiency.
